title: LCA of Coffee Cups and Takeaway Packaging: Single-use, Compostable and Reusable
sub: A cradle-to-grave comparison of a single-use paper cup, a compostable cup, a reusable cup and a ceramic cup, showing how many uses a reusable cup needs to pay off.
pdf: Case 10 — LCA of Coffee Cups and Takeaway Packaging: Executive Summary
fu: Serving one 350 ml hot drink in a container (cup and lid), takeaway or in-café, in Germany; the coffee itself is excluded
ref: Baseline: one 11 g paperboard cup with 0.6 g PE lining and a 3 g polystyrene lid. Alternatives: PLA-lined cup with CPLA lid; 1/50 of a 100 g reusable PP cup plus washing; 1/1,000 of a 350 g ceramic cup plus commercial dishwashing
boundary: Cradle-to-grave: paperboard and polymer production, cup forming and printing, distribution to cafés, use (washing for reusables), collection and transport, recycling, composting, incineration and landfill
geo: Cup production in Europe; use and waste management in Germany
method: EF 3.1 characterisation; IPCC AR6 GWP100; AWARE for water scarcity
alloc: Reusable cups: production and end-of-life divided by number of uses; washing allocated per use (shared dishwasher loads); recycling via cut-off; biogenic carbon neutral except methane from landfilled paper
cutoff: Flows <1% of mass and energy excluded (sleeves, stirrers, napkins) with cumulative exclusions <5%
dq: UNEP (2021) beverage-cup meta-analysis, JRC (2024) packaging study, ecoinvent, published reusable-cup LCAs; washing energy from appliance data. Overall data quality Medium; Low for consumer washing behaviour
srcShort: Illustrative model; parameters within ranges from the UNEP (2021) meta-analysis of beverage-cup LCAs, the JRC (2024) single-use vs multiple-use packaging study, ecoinvent and published reusable-cup LCAs.
loop: Circular loop: reusable cups washed and returned; paper fibre recovered only in specialist facilities
exec:
This case study compares four ways of serving a 350 ml hot drink: a single-use PE-lined paper cup with a polystyrene lid, a compostable PLA-lined cup, a reusable polypropylene cup used 50 times and washed at home, and a ceramic cup used 1,000 times in a café. Single-use cups are targeted by the Single-Use Plastics Directive (labelling and consumption reduction) and the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation, which requires takeaway businesses to offer customers the option of bringing their own container.
The illustrative single-use baseline is 0.050 kg CO2e per drink. The paperboard (24%), lining and lid (22%) and end-of-life (30%, including methane from landfilled paper and incinerated plastic) are the main contributors. The compostable cup performs about the same, because its benefit depends on industrial composting that most cups never reach.
The reusable PP cup reaches 0.029 kg CO2e at 50 uses (−43%), and the ceramic cup 0.013 kg (−75%). However, reusables use more water for washing, and a reusable cup only beats a single-use cup after about 15 uses.
Recommendations focus on in-café reusable service, deposit-based reusable cup systems and lid redesign, rather than material substitution. For CSRD, results support ESRS E5 (packaging and waste), E1 (Scope 3) and E2 (plastic linings and litter).
overview:
Takeaway coffee cups are made from paperboard with a thin plastic lining to make them waterproof, plus a plastic lid. The lining makes recycling difficult, and compostable variants require separate collection and industrial composting.
The purpose of this LCA is to test common assumptions (that compostable is better and that reusables always win) and to identify break-even conditions for reuse.
goal: The goal is to support a coffee chain's packaging and service model decisions. The audience is operations, procurement, sustainability and marketing teams. Results are not intended for public comparative claims without critical review.

hot.why: Landfilled paper releases methane; incinerated linings and lids release fossil CO2. End-of-life is 30% of the result because lined cups are rarely recycled.
Food-grade virgin board is the largest material input and the main water and land contributor.
The 3 g polystyrene lid makes up most of the liner-and-lid stage (about a fifth of the total), and polystyrene is rarely recycled.
For reusable cups, washing becomes the dominant impact; hot water and inefficient washing can erase their benefits.

PLA-lined cup with CPLA lid; only 5% reaches industrial composting, the rest is incinerated or landfilled

350 g ceramic cup used in-café, washed in an efficient commercial dishwasher

sens.t: Sensitivity: number of uses of the reusable PP cup
sens.xl: Number of uses per reusable cup
sens.note: The reusable cup's benefit depends on the number of uses and on how it is washed.
sens.interp: With dishwasher washing, the reusable cup breaks even after about 15 uses; with a cold rinse, after about 9. Many reusable cups bought on impulse are used fewer times than this.

wf: Switch to reusable PP cup (50 uses)

ci.stage: End-of-life, paperboard and the lid are the main contributors for single-use cups.
ci.stage_e: Polymer production for the lid and lining is the largest energy contributor.
ci.stage_w: Water consumption comes mainly from paperboard production.
ci.donut: Nearly a third of the single-use result occurs after the cup is used, driven by landfill methane and plastic incineration.
ci.sankey: Of each 14.6 g cup and lid, less than 1 g is recycled; most is incinerated or landfilled.
ci.heat: Cup material is the hotspot for water and land; liner and lid for energy and resources; end-of-life for climate.
ci.scen: Compostable cups do not reduce impacts under current waste infrastructure; reusables reduce climate impact if used enough.
ci.radar: Reusables are lowest on climate, energy, waste and land but highest on water because of washing.
ci.wf: Switching to reuse delivers the largest reduction; how cups are washed is the second lever.

interp.m: Reusable and in-café ceramic cups reduce climate impact and waste substantially when used many times; compostable single-use cups offer little benefit without composting infrastructure.
interp.a: Number of uses; washing method and energy; end-of-life routes (landfill share); lid material.
interp.u: Consumer washing behaviour and actual use counts are poorly known; landfill methane factors vary.
interp.can: Reuse at high rotation is the main lever; compostable claims need infrastructure evidence; lids matter.
interp.cannot: The study cannot claim that every reusable cup is better; low-use reusables can be worse. It does not quantify litter impacts.
interp.d: In-café 'for here' defaults, deposit-based reusable cup schemes, lid redesign, procurement of single-use cups, avoiding unsupported compostability claims.

recs: Design durable, easy-to-clean reusable cups; replace polystyrene lids with recyclable mono-material or fibre lids; avoid compostable formats without a composting route.
Buy reusable systems with tracked rotation rates; for single-use, specify recyclable linings where collection exists.
Use certified fibre and renewable energy; develop aqueous-dispersion barrier coatings that are recyclable.
Make ceramic cups the default for in-café drinks; offer deposit-based reusable cups and discounts for own cups (PPWR requires a bring-your-own option).
Provide cup-collection points with specialist recycling; avoid mixing compostable cups with recycling streams.
Track reusable rotation rates and single-use cup volumes; review compostable and recyclable claims under green-claims rules.
Support reuse systems and consumption-reduction measures; ensure compostability claims match infrastructure.

take: A reusable cup is only better once it has been used enough: around 15 uses with dishwasher washing; in-café ceramic service gives the largest reduction, while compostable cups offer little benefit without composting infrastructure.
biz: Make ceramic the default for in-café drinks, run a deposit-based reusable cup scheme with tracked rotation rates, replace polystyrene lids, and avoid compostability claims that local infrastructure cannot support.
